antipsychotics.name: Antipsychotics
antipsychotics.scope: First-generation vs second-generation, extrapyramidal symptoms (acute dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia), neuroleptic malignant syndrome, metabolic syndrome, hyperprolactinemia, QTc prolongation
antipsychotics.core: Dopamine-modulating drugs treat psychosis and mania; selection depends on motor, metabolic, endocrine, cardiovascular, and hematologic risks.

rows.label: Use
items: ★ Psychosis, mania, severe agitation; **clozapine** for resistant schizophrenia or recurrent suicidality
FGA: mainly D2 antagonism; SGA: D2/5-HT2 effects, varying by agent

rows.label: Mechanism
items: Nigrostriatal blockade → movement disorders; tuberoinfundibular blockade → prolactin elevation
Aripiprazole: partial D2 agonist; haloperidol high-potency FGA, chlorpromazine low-potency FGA

rows.label: Adverse
items: ★ Fever, **lead-pipe rigidity**, autonomic instability, high CK → NMS; stop drug, supportive ICU care
Severe NMS: dantrolene/bromocriptine; olanzapine/clozapine: weight gain, diabetes, dyslipidemia
Risperidone: ↑prolactin; ziprasidone: ↑QT; clozapine: neutropenia, myocarditis, ileus, seizures

rows.label: Avoid
items: Lewy body/Parkinson disease: severe sensitivity; specialist-selected quetiapine/clozapine if essential
Dementia: increased mortality; reserve for dangerous/severely distressing behavior after safer measures

rows.label: Interactions
items: Other QT-prolonging drugs, electrolyte depletion → torsades; sedatives/alcohol increase CNS depression

rows.label: Monitor
items: ★ Weight/BMI, BP, glucose/A1c, lipids; movement examinations; **ANC with clozapine**
ECG for cardiac/QT risks; prolactin when symptomatic; ask about bowel function

rows.label: Traps

rows.label: Risk factors

Prior cranial radiation; NF 2 predisposes to bilateral vestibular schwannomas and meningiomas

rows.label: Clues

Frontal lesions → personality change; motor cortex → weakness; posterior fossa → ataxia

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Tumor disrupts local brain function and blood–brain barrier → vasogenic edema
Fixed cranial volume makes expanding tissue/CSF raise pressure and threaten brainstem perfusion

rows.label: Dx

Metastatic pattern → search primary with chest/abdominal imaging; tissue diagnosis when needed
★ Suspected mass with pressure signs → **avoid LP** until safe after imaging
Vestibular symptoms → audiometry and MRI internal auditory canals

Seizure → levetiracetam; no routine antiseizure prophylaxis for every seizure-naive tumor patient
★ **Resection versus radiation** depends on lesion, symptoms, accessibility and systemic disease
Medulloblastoma → resection, chemotherapy and usually craniospinal radiation; avoid/delay radiation in very young children

rows.label: Complications
items: Obstructive hydrocephalus, herniation, hemorrhage, persistent neurologic deficits

rows.label: Mimics

carbon-monoxide-poisoning.name: Carbon monoxide poisoning
carbon-monoxide-poisoning.scope: Carboxyhemoglobin, pulse oximetry pitfall, normobaric and hyperbaric oxygen indications, delayed neurologic sequelae
carbon-monoxide-poisoning.core: Headache, dizziness, nausea, or confusion affecting several people in an enclosed combustion setting suggests carbon monoxide exposure.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: House fires, faulty heaters, generators indoors, vehicle exhaust, poorly ventilated fuel-burning equipment
Pregnancy, infancy, anemia, and cardiopulmonary disease increase vulnerability at a given exposure

rows.label: Clues
items: Flulike illness without fever; symptoms improve outside exposure site
★ **Syncope, altered consciousness, focal deficits, chest pain**, or severe acidosis → serious toxicity
Cherry-red skin uncommon; ordinary skin color offers no reassurance

rows.label: Pathophys
items: CO binds hemoglobin avidly, reduces oxygen carriage, shifts dissociation curve left
Mitochondrial dysfunction and inflammation add tissue injury; fetal hemoglobin retains CO longer

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Venous or arterial co-oximetry** measures carboxyhemoglobin; draw promptly without delaying oxygen
★ **Normal pulse oximetry and PaO₂ do not exclude poisoning**; both can appear reassuring
COHb >2% in nonsmokers or >9% in smokers supports exposure; level poorly predicts outcome
ECG, troponin for cardiac injury; lactate/ABG for acidosis; pregnancy testing when relevant
Prior oxygen or delayed presentation lowers COHb; exposure history remains decisive

rows.label: Tx
items: Remove from source, protect rescuers, assess airway and ventilation
★ **100% oxygen by nonrebreather** immediately; intubate for coma or respiratory failure
Consider hyperbaric oxygen for neurologic impairment, loss of consciousness, cardiac injury, severe acidosis, or COHb >25–30%
Pregnancy → urgent hyperbaric consultation at lower severity/levels; treatment decisions integrate symptoms, not COHb alone
Smoke inhalation + profound lactic acidosis/shock → consider cyanide, give hydroxocobalamin

rows.label: Complications
items: Myocardial ischemia, arrhythmias, death; delayed cognitive, behavioral, gait, or movement deficits after recovery
Follow-up for delayed neurologic symptoms; mild initial presentation does not exclude later deficits

rows.label: Prevention
items: Working CO detectors, professional heater inspection, never run generators or engines indoors
Public safety evaluation before returning to the exposure site

rows.label: Mimics
items: Viral illness: fever and infectious contacts rather than shared building exposure
Methemoglobinemia: cyanosis, saturation near 85%, chocolate-colored blood
Cyanide poisoning: rapid collapse, marked lactate elevation after enclosed fire

carotid-artery-stenosis.scope: Asymptomatic carotid bruit, carotid duplex ultrasound, medical management, indications for carotid endarterectomy

rows.label: Risk factors

rows.label: Dx

delirium.name: Delirium
delirium.scope: Diagnostic criteria, precipitating causes (infection, metabolic, drugs), workup, management and prevention
delirium.core: Acute fluctuating inattention with altered cognition or awareness indicates delirium and requires a search for physiologic triggers.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older age, baseline dementia, frailty, sensory impairment, hospitalization or recent surgery
Infection, hypoxia, metabolic derangement, dehydration, retention, constipation and uncontrolled pain
Anticholinergics, opioids, sedatives; alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal

rows.label: Clues

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Systemic stress and drug effects disrupt vulnerable brain networks and neurotransmitter balance

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CAM**: acute/fluctuating course + inattention + disorganized thinking or altered consciousness
Immediate glucose, oxygenation, vitals; focused neurologic examination, medication review and collateral baseline

items: ★ **Treat precipitant**; reorient, restore hearing/glasses, hydrate, mobilize and normalize sleep

dementia.name: Dementia
dementia.scope: Alzheimer, vascular, Lewy body, frontotemporal, reversible causes, normal cognitive aging vs MCI, Parkinson disease dementia
dementia.core: Acquired cognitive decline interfering with independent daily function; distinguish dementia from normal aging and mild cognitive impairment by functional consequences.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Advanced age, family history; vascular risk factors, prior stroke, Parkinson disease

rows.label: Clues
items: Collateral history: missed bills/medications, getting lost, unsafe cooking or driving

rows.label: Pathophys

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Patient/informant history, cognition, function**; MoCA/MMSE support diagnosis, cannot establish it alone
★ **CBC, CMP, TSH, B12**, depression/medication review; HIV/syphilis testing if risk
Brain MRI or noncontrast CT → infarcts, mass, subdural, hydrocephalus; avoid routine PET as first test
Normal aging: slower retrieval with preserved independence; MCI: objective deficit without loss of independent function

items: ★ Alzheimer/Lewy/Parkinson dementia → **donepezil or rivastigmine**; moderate/severe Alzheimer → add memantine
Vascular disease → BP/lipid/diabetes control, stroke prevention; frontotemporal behavioral symptoms → consider SSRI
★ Agitation → seek pain/infection, routines/redirection first; **avoid typical antipsychotics in Lewy disease**

items: Falls, aspiration, malnutrition, wandering, caregiver burnout; antipsychotics → increased mortality
Cholinesterase inhibitors → bradycardia, syncope, GI effects; antiamyloid antibodies → edema/microhemorrhage

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Driving/home safety, advance planning**, caregiver support; assess decision-specific capacity

Severe autoimmune disease: arrhythmia, hypoventilation, prolonged rehabilitation

rows.label: Prevention
items: Mosquito repellent, protective clothing, vector control; no routine HSV encephalitis vaccine

rows.label: Mimics
items: Bacterial meningitis: neutrophilic CSF, low glucose; overlap requires empiric coverage
Toxic/metabolic delirium: systemic explanation without inflammatory CSF
Primary psychosis: lacks new seizures, dysautonomia, or focal neurologic abnormalities

encephalitis.evidence: Not checked online; established infectious and autoimmune neurology teaching.

epilepsy.name: Epilepsy
epilepsy.scope: Focal seizures, generalized tonic-clonic seizures, absence seizures, juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, EEG findings, antiepileptic therapy (valproate, levetiracetam, lamotrigine), lifestyle counseling
epilepsy.core: Recurrent unprovoked seizures reflect epilepsy; classify focal versus generalized onset before choosing a maintenance antiseizure drug.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior brain injury, stroke, CNS infection, developmental lesions, genetic predisposition
Sleep deprivation, alcohol withdrawal and missed drugs can precipitate seizures; provoked seizures alone ≠ epilepsy

rows.label: Clues
items: Focal onset: aura, unilateral motor activity, automatisms or impaired awareness; may evolve bilaterally
Generalized tonic-clonic: abrupt loss of consciousness, stiffening/jerking, postictal confusion, lateral tongue injury
Absence: staring, immediate recovery; JME: morning myoclonus ± generalized convulsions

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Abnormally synchronized cortical neuronal discharges impair awareness, sensation or motor function
Excitatory/inhibitory imbalance may arise from structural lesions or inherited channel/network dysfunction

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **EEG and epilepsy-protocol MRI** after unprovoked seizure; normal EEG does not exclude epilepsy
Epilepsy: ≥2 unprovoked seizures >24 hours apart, or one with high recurrence risk/defined syndrome
Check glucose/electrolytes and provoking causes; urgent CT for trauma, focal deficit or persistent altered consciousness
Absence: generalized **3-Hz spike-wave**, provoked by hyperventilation; JME: generalized polyspike-wave

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Convulsion **≥5 minutes** → airway/glucose, **lorazepam**, then IV levetiracetam/fosphenytoin/valproate
Focal epilepsy → lamotrigine or levetiracetam; generalized tonic-clonic/JME → broad-spectrum agent
★ Valproate effective for generalized syndromes; **avoid when pregnancy possible** if alternatives effective
Pure absence → ethosuximide; absence plus generalized tonic-clonic → broad-spectrum drug
Avoid carbamazepine/phenytoin for absence/myoclonic syndromes; drug-resistant focal disease → surgical evaluation

rows.label: Complications
items: Status epilepticus, injury, aspiration, SUDEP; valproate → hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, teratogenicity
Lamotrigine → serious rash with rapid titration; levetiracetam → irritability/mood symptoms

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Adherence, regular sleep, avoid alcohol excess; no abrupt drug withdrawal
Driving restrictions follow local law; no unsupervised swimming/heights; preconception folate and drug review

rows.label: Mimics
items: Syncope: prodrome, rapid recovery; brief jerks possible
Psychogenic nonepileptic events: video-EEG confirms typical event without epileptic correlate

epilepsy.evidence: Pregnancy recommendations checked 2026-10-30: [AAN/AES/SMFM 2024](https://www.aan.com/PressRoom/Home/PressRelease/5170); classification established teaching.

gait-impairment-and-falls.name: Gait impairment and falls in older adults
gait-impairment-and-falls.scope: Multifactorial fall risk assessment, Get Up and Go test, chair rise test, muscle weakness, sensory deficits, physical therapy
gait-impairment-and-falls.core: Falls in older adults usually reflect interacting gait, medication, sensory, cardiovascular, and environmental risks; assess causes and restore safe mobility.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior fall, frailty, lower-extremity weakness, neuropathy, impaired vision/hearing, cognitive impairment
Sedatives, anticholinergics, opioids, polypharmacy, orthostatic medications; unsafe footwear or home hazards

rows.label: Clues
items: Slow rising, broad-based or shuffling gait, unstable turning, fear of falling
Ask about prodrome, loss of consciousness, exertion, palpitations, urinary urgency, and prolonged floor time
★ **Focal deficit, syncope, head injury, inability to bear weight** → targeted urgent assessment

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Reduced strength, proprioception, vision, or vestibular function undermines compensatory postural responses
Fear-driven inactivity worsens deconditioning and increases future risk

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Timed Up and Go**: rise, walk 3 m, turn, return, sit; ≥12 seconds suggests risk
Chair-rise test assesses leg strength; Romberg, gait observation, neurologic and foot examinations localize deficits
★ **Orthostatic BP, medication review, vision assessment**, footwear and home-safety review
CBC, glucose, ECG, electrolytes only when history suggests causes; no routine head imaging for uncomplicated falls

rows.label: Tx
items: Treat injury and acute cause; correct dehydration or orthostasis
★ **PT: balance, strength, gait training**, properly fitted cane/walker
Deprescribe fall-promoting drugs; correct vision and footwear; occupational therapist for home modifications
Manage neuropathy, arthritis, Parkinson disease; assess osteoporosis and nutritional deficiency
Vitamin D for deficiency, not universal supplementation solely to prevent falls

rows.label: Complications
items: Hip fracture, subdural hemorrhage, rhabdomyolysis after prolonged immobility
Loss of independence, institutionalization, anxiety; restrictive immobilization can worsen function

rows.label: Prevention
items: Regular multicomponent exercise; remove rugs/clutter, improve lighting, install grab bars
Review recurrence, emergency alert access, safe transfers and toileting; avoid routine physical restraints

rows.label: Mimics
items: Syncope: transient loss of consciousness from cardiac/orthostatic causes
Normal-pressure hydrocephalus: magnetic gait, cognitive decline, incontinence
Cerebellar disorder: ataxia persists with eyes open, dysmetria

gait-impairment-and-falls.evidence: Not checked online; established geriatric assessment teaching.

geriatric-assessment.name: Geriatric assessment
geriatric-assessment.scope: Comprehensive geriatric assessment, activities of daily living, instrumental ADLs, home safety, multidisciplinary care
geriatric-assessment.core: Comprehensive geriatric assessment integrates medical, functional, cognitive, psychological, and social findings into a coordinated plan aligned with the older adult’s goals.

rows.label: Definition
items: Identify reversible contributors to frailty, disability, drug harms, and unsafe living
Domains: gait, cognition, mood, nutrition, continence, senses, drugs, caregivers, home

rows.label: Interpret
items: ★ **IADL decline often precedes ADL decline**; establish baseline and change over time
Dependence identifies support needs; disability does not alone establish incapacity

rows.label: Use when
items: ★ New falls, functional loss, recurrent hospitalization, weight loss, polypharmacy, or caregiver strain
Ask patient goals; reconcile prescriptions, OTC drugs, supplements, adherence, and affordability
Assess home hazards, food access, transportation, social isolation, and suspected abuse

rows.label: Compare
items: ADLs: bathing, dressing, toileting, transferring, continence, feeding
IADLs: medications, finances, shopping, cooking, transport, housekeeping, communication
Screen cognition and depression; interpret performance in context of hearing, vision, education, language

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Acute cognitive change → delirium assessment**, not automatic dementia labeling
Chronologic age alone should not decide surgery, rehabilitation, or preventive care
★ Combine **PT/OT, nursing, pharmacy, social work**, and primary care into one prioritized plan

geriatric-assessment.evidence: Definitions and established geriatric practice; not checked online.

hiv-infection.name: HIV infection
hiv-infection.scope: Acute HIV, testing, ART start, opportunistic infection prophylaxis, PrEP/PEP, opportunistic infections (CMV retinitis, toxoplasmosis, PJP)
hiv-infection.core: HIV progressively depletes CD4 cells; early diagnosis and suppressive ART prevent immune failure and sexual transmission.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Sexual exposure, shared injection equipment, perinatal transmission; other STIs increase acquisition risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Acute infection: fever, rash, sore throat, generalized lymphadenopathy after recent exposure
Weight loss, oral thrush, recurrent infections suggest advanced immunodeficiency

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Retroviral integration creates lifelong reservoirs; ongoing replication drives immune depletion and inflammation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Fourth-generation Ag/Ab → HIV-1/2 differentiation assay**; discordance → HIV RNA
★ Recent exposure/acute syndrome despite negative screen → **HIV RNA**, before antibodies appear
Baseline viral load, CD4, resistance genotype, renal/liver function, HBV/HCV/TB testing; pregnancy assessment
AIDS: CD4 <200 or AIDS-defining illness regardless of count

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Start **integrase-based ART promptly**, usually bictegravir/TAF/emtricitabine; assess HBV coinfection and interactions
Do not delay routine ART for genotype; cryptococcal/TB meningitis require disease-specific deferred timing
PJP: TMP-SMX; add glucocorticoid if PaO₂ <70 or A–a gradient ≥35
Toxoplasmosis: pyrimethamine/sulfadiazine/leucovorin or TMP-SMX; CMV retinitis: valganciclovir, urgent ophthalmology

rows.label: Complications
items: Opportunistic infections, malignancies, wasting, neurocognitive disease, kidney disease
Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome after ART; drug toxicity/interactions

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ PJP prophylaxis: **TMP-SMX** with CD4 <200 before/starting ART; on ART, <100 or 100–200 with viremia
Toxoplasma IgG positive + CD4 <100 → prophylaxis; MAC <50 only without immediate effective ART
★ Exposure ≤72 hours → **28-day PEP: dolutegravir + TDF/emtricitabine**; do not delay for laboratory results
PrEP: TDF/emtricitabine, cabotegravir, or lenacapavir; exclude HIV first, continue serial testing

rows.label: Mimics
items: EBV mononucleosis: atypical lymphocytes, heterophile positivity; acute HIV can be heterophile-negative
Primary CNS lymphoma: often solitary brain lesion, fails empiric anti-Toxoplasma treatment

table.title: Advanced-disease syndromes
rows: Dry cough, hypoxemia, ground-glass; induced sputum/BAL

huntington-disease.name: Huntington disease
huntington-disease.scope: CAG trinucleotide repeat expansion, anticipation, chorea, caudate and putamen atrophy, psychiatric manifestations
huntington-disease.core: An inherited progressive movement, cognitive, and psychiatric disorder often emerges in midlife, with earlier onset across successive generations.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: ★ **Autosomal dominant HTT CAG expansion**; each child of an affected heterozygote has 50% risk
Paternal transmission particularly associated with repeat expansion and anticipation

rows.label: Clues
items: Irregular flowing chorea, motor impersistence, impaired voluntary saccades; later rigidity and bradykinesia
Irritability, depression, impulsivity, psychosis; executive dysfunction progresses to dementia
Psychiatric symptoms may precede movement disorder; juvenile disease often rigid with seizures
★ **Suicidal ideation** requires direct safety assessment, especially around diagnosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Toxic huntingtin damages striatal GABAergic neurons; reduced indirect-pathway inhibition increases unwanted movement
Caudate/putamen atrophy produces enlarged frontal horns on brain imaging

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Compatible phenotype/family history → **HTT genetic testing** after informed counseling
≥40 repeats: full penetrance; 36–39: reduced penetrance; intermediate alleles can expand in offspring
MRI supports differential diagnosis; gene testing confirms, imaging alone does not
Predictive testing of asymptomatic adults → consent, psychological assessment and genetic counseling

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Disabling chorea → **tetrabenazine or deutetrabenazine**; monitor depression, suicidality and parkinsonism
Antipsychotics such as risperidone for psychosis/aggression; SSRIs for depression/anxiety
Physical/occupational and speech-swallow support; nutrition, fall prevention and advance-care planning
No established cure; avoid dopamine-depleting agents in active suicidality or inadequately treated depression

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration pneumonia, falls, weight loss, loss of independence; suicide
VMAT2 inhibitors → sedation, akathisia, depression; antipsychotics → metabolic and motor adverse effects

rows.label: Prevention
items: Reproductive counseling, prenatal/preimplantation testing options; defer predictive testing of asymptomatic minors

rows.label: Mimics
items: Wilson disease: younger onset, liver disease, low ceruloplasmin; potentially treatable
Tardive dyskinesia: dopamine-blocker exposure, predominant orobuccolingual stereotypies

huntington-disease.evidence: Not checked online; established clinical teaching.

hypertensive-crises.name: Hypertensive crises
hypertensive-crises.scope: Hypertensive urgency, hypertensive emergency, hypertensive encephalopathy, aortic dissection, acute pulmonary edema, IV labetalol, nicardipine, nitroprusside
hypertensive-crises.core: Severe BP elevation becomes an emergency when new target-organ injury accompanies it; the number alone does not determine urgency.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Missed antihypertensives, CKD, sympathomimetics; clonidine withdrawal
Pregnancy, renovascular disease, catecholamine excess

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Usually **>180/120 mm Hg** with AKI, ACS, pulmonary edema, stroke, or dissection
Encephalopathy: headache, confusion, seizures, visual disturbance; papilledema or retinal hemorrhages

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Autoregulatory failure → endothelial injury, microangiopathy, tissue ischemia; cerebral vasogenic edema in PRES

rows.label: Dx
items: Repeat correctly sized cuff reading; examine neurologic status, fundi, pulses, heart and lungs
Creatinine, electrolytes, urinalysis, ECG; troponin with cardiac symptoms
Neurologic symptoms → head CT; suspected dissection → CTA chest/aorta
MRI posterior vasogenic edema supports PRES after hemorrhage exclusion

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Most emergencies: ICU, titratable IV **nicardipine or labetalol**
★ Reduce MAP ≤25% first hour → approximately 160/100–110 over 2–6 hours; then gradual normalization
★ No acute injury: treat pain/anxiety, restart or adjust oral drugs, arrange close outpatient follow-up
Avoid rapid IV lowering for asymptomatic BP; avoid immediate-release nifedipine
Nitroprusside: cyanide/thiocyanate toxicity with prolonged use or renal/hepatic dysfunction; monitor closely

rows.label: Complications
items: Cerebral hemorrhage, renal failure, MI; overly rapid lowering → cerebral/coronary hypoperfusion

rows.label: Prevention
items: Medication access and adherence; home BP monitoring; avoid cocaine and amphetamines

rows.label: Mimics
items: Pain/anxiety elevation: improves after trigger control, no acute injury
Ischemic stroke: permissive hypertension thresholds differ; avoid applying generic reduction targets

increased-intracranial-pressure.name: Increased intracranial pressure
increased-intracranial-pressure.scope: Cushing triad, papilledema, ventriculoperitoneal shunt malfunction, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, herniation syndromes, hyperosmolar therapy
increased-intracranial-pressure.core: Progressive headache, vomiting, or depressed consciousness from raised intracranial pressure requires rapid distinction between mass effect, hydrocephalus, and idiopathic intracranial hypertension.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Trauma, intracranial bleeding, tumor, cerebral edema, CNS infection, obstructed CSF flow
VP shunt: blockage or infection; IIH: obesity, reproductive-age women, tetracyclines, retinoids

rows.label: Clues
items: Morning/Valsalva headache, papilledema, diplopia from sixth-nerve palsy; infants may have bulging fontanelle
★ **Cushing triad**: hypertension/widened pulse pressure, bradycardia, irregular respirations; late dangerous finding
Uncal herniation → ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil, contralateral weakness; tonsillar herniation → respiratory arrest
IIH: pulsatile tinnitus, transient visual obscurations; shunt failure: recurrent headache, vomiting, lethargy

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Fixed skull volume: excess tissue, blood, or CSF raises pressure after compensatory reserve exhausted
Cerebral perfusion pressure = MAP − ICP; falling perfusion worsens ischemia and edema

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Unstable/acute deficit → **noncontrast head CT**; papilledema with stable suspected IIH → MRI + MRV
★ **No LP before excluding mass effect/obstructive hydrocephalus** when concerning signs present
IIH: normal imaging aside from supportive findings, normal CSF composition, opening pressure ≥25 cm H₂O
Shunt failure → head imaging, shunt series, urgent neurosurgery; normal ventricular size does not exclude obstruction

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Herniation concern → **airway support, head elevation, IV hypertonic saline or mannitol**, urgent neurosurgery
Avoid hypoxia/hypotension; brief controlled hyperventilation only as bridge for impending herniation
Hydrocephalus → CSF drainage/shunt revision; mass lesion → definitive decompression
Dexamethasone for tumor-associated vasogenic edema; no corticosteroids for traumatic brain injury
IIH → weight loss + acetazolamide; threatened vision → optic nerve fenestration or CSF diversion

rows.label: Complications
items: Permanent visual loss, ischemic injury, herniation, death
Hyperosmolar agents → electrolyte/renal disturbances; CSF devices → infection

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid causative drugs in IIH; follow visual fields and optic discs
Shunt education: prompt evaluation for recurrence or fever; injury prevention

rows.label: Mimics
items: Migraine: normal fundus and no progressive focal/mental-status findings
Cerebral venous thrombosis: venous obstruction on MRV, not idiopathic disease

increased-intracranial-pressure.evidence: Not checked online; established neurocritical care and IIH diagnostic principles.

inflammatory-myopathies.name: Inflammatory myopathies
inflammatory-myopathies.scope: Polymyositis, dermatomyositis, inclusion body myositis, elevated creatine kinase, autoantibodies (anti-Jo-1, anti-Mi-2), muscle biopsy, malignancy screening, systemic corticosteroids
inflammatory-myopathies.core: Objective muscle weakness with elevated muscle enzymes suggests myopathy; distribution, skin findings, and biopsy distinguish treatable inflammation from inclusion body disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Autoimmune predisposition; adult dermatomyositis associated with occult malignancy
Inclusion body myositis: usually men >50 years; review statin and other myotoxic exposures

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Difficulty rising or lifting arms**, neck flexor weakness; sensation generally preserved
Dysphagia, aspiration, dyspnea warrant evaluation for bulbar/respiratory weakness and interstitial lung disease
Dermatomyositis can have characteristic rash before significant muscle weakness

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Polymyositis: T-cell-mediated endomysial injury; dermatomyositis: complement-associated microvascular injury
Inclusion body disease combines inflammatory and degenerative pathology, explaining poor immunosuppressive response

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CK, aldolase, AST/ALT**, TSH; muscle can explain transaminase elevation without primary liver disease
MRI identifies edema and guides **muscle biopsy**; EMG supports a myopathic pattern
★ **Anti-Jo-1**: antisynthetase syndrome with ILD, arthritis, mechanic's hands; **anti-Mi-2**: classic dermatomyositis
Check swallowing and lung function when symptomatic; exclude inherited, endocrine, and drug-induced myopathies

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Polymyositis/dermatomyositis → **systemic glucocorticoids + steroid-sparing agent**, such as methotrexate or azathioprine
Severe/refractory disease or dysphagia → IVIG or other specialist-directed immunomodulation
Inclusion body: PT/OT, mobility aids, swallowing support; immunosuppression usually ineffective
Dermatomyositis rash: sun protection and topical agents; rehabilitation without prolonged immobilization

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration pneumonia, respiratory failure, ILD, myocarditis; juvenile dermatomyositis can cause calcinosis
Steroid myopathy causes new weakness with normal CK; treatment also increases infection and fracture risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Adult dermatomyositis → **age-based plus risk-based malignancy evaluation**, especially near diagnosis
Bone protection, immunizations, infection prophylaxis according to immunosuppressive intensity; monitor strength and CK

rows.label: Mimics
items: Polymyalgia rheumatica: pain/stiffness without true weakness or ↑CK
Myasthenia: fatigability, ocular symptoms, normal CK; ALS: mixed UMN/LMN signs

table.title: Distribution and biopsy
rows: Heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, shawl erythema

ischemic-stroke-and-tia.name: Ischemic stroke and TIA
ischemic-stroke-and-tia.scope: TIA (including amaurosis fugax), ischemic stroke, acute management (tPA, thrombectomy), secondary prevention, risk factors
ischemic-stroke-and-tia.core: Abrupt focal neurologic loss from cerebral ischemia; transient monocular blindness localizes to the ipsilateral carotid circulation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Hypertension, smoking, diabetes, dyslipidemia, carotid atherosclerosis
Atrial fibrillation, recent MI, endocarditis, arterial dissection

rows.label: Clues
items: Aphasia or neglect suggests cortical involvement; crossed cranial-nerve/limb findings suggest brainstem disease
★ **Last known well** establishes treatment timing; symptom discovery time may differ
TIA: resolved deficit without acute infarction; urgent evaluation despite normal examination

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Thromboembolism or small-vessel occlusion → infarct core surrounded by salvageable penumbra
Reperfusion preserves threatened tissue but increases hemorrhagic transformation risk

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Fingerstick glucose + **noncontrast head CT** first; normal early CT does not exclude ischemia
CTA head/neck for large-vessel occlusion; MRI diffusion for small infarcts or diagnostic uncertainty
ECG, telemetry, carotid imaging; echocardiography for suspected cardiac emboli

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Disabling deficit, eligible ≤4.5 hours → **alteplase or tenecteplase**; imaging-selected extended windows possible
Thrombolysis: BP <185/110 before, <180/105 after; exclude bleeding and significant anticoagulant effect
★ Large-vessel occlusion → **mechanical thrombectomy**, selected cases through 24 hours; do not delay thrombolysis
No reperfusion: generally allow BP ≤220/120; oxygen for hypoxemia; swallow assessment before oral intake
Aspirin after hemorrhage excluded; after thrombolysis, wait 24 hours and repeat imaging

rows.label: Complications
items: Cerebral edema, aspiration, venous thrombosis, seizures, disability

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Minor noncardioembolic stroke/high-risk TIA → short **aspirin + clopidogrel**, then single antiplatelet
AF → oral anticoagulation with timing based on infarct/bleeding risk; high-intensity statin, BP control
Symptomatic carotid stenosis 70–99% → endarterectomy when eligible; selected 50–69% also benefit

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hypoglycemia: deficit reverses with glucose
Migraine aura: spreading positive symptoms; seizure: witnessed convulsion followed by Todd paralysis

low-back-pain.name: Low back pain
low-back-pain.scope: Lumbosacral strain, herniated disk and radiculopathy, spinal stenosis, red flags, imaging indications, conservative management
low-back-pain.core: Most acute low back pain improves with activity and analgesia; neurologic deficits or systemic red flags change the workup.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Heavy lifting, deconditioning, obesity, prolonged sitting
Cancer, immunosuppression, injection drug use, osteoporosis, chronic glucocorticoids increase serious-pathology risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Mechanical pain varies with movement; isolated axial pain without systemic illness favors benign disease
★ **Urinary retention, saddle anesthesia, bilateral weakness** → cauda equina emergency
Fever, weight loss, night pain, trauma, or progressive weakness → targeted urgent evaluation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Paraspinal injury causes localized pain; degenerative narrowing or disk extrusion compresses neural structures

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ No red flags → **no initial imaging**, including routine radiographs
Focused strength, reflex, sensory, gait examination; straight-leg raise supports lower lumbar radiculopathy
★ Suspected infection, malignancy, cord compression → **MRI**; suspected fracture → radiograph or CT
Persistent symptoms despite about 6 weeks' care → MRI if intervention being considered
Suspected spinal infection → ESR/CRP, blood cultures; normal temperature does not exclude infection

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Continue activity**, superficial heat, short NSAID course; avoid prolonged bed rest
Physical rehabilitation for persistent symptoms; avoid routine opioids and systemic steroids
Progressive motor deficit or cauda equina → urgent surgical decompression
Refractory disabling radicular pain → epidural injection or diskectomy after imaging correlation

rows.label: Complications
items: Chronic pain, functional limitation, medication dependence
Untreated compression → permanent bladder, bowel, sexual, or motor dysfunction

rows.label: Prevention
items: Core strengthening, regular exercise, ergonomic lifting, weight management
Return to usual tasks gradually; address fear avoidance and workplace barriers

rows.label: Mimics
items: AAA: abdominal pulsatile mass, vascular risk, hypotension
Renal colic: flank-to-groin pain, hematuria; inflammatory back pain: improves with exercise

table.title: Mechanical patterns
rows: Leg pain below knee; cough aggravates

low-back-pain.evidence: Not checked online; established generalist back-pain evaluation.

lyme-disease.name: Lyme disease
lyme-disease.scope: Borrelia burgdorferi, erythema migrans, early localized, early disseminated, late Lyme arthritis, doxycycline, ceftriaxone
lyme-disease.core: Ixodes-transmitted Borrelia infection progresses from an expanding skin lesion to neurologic, cardiac, or joint disease when untreated.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Wooded/brush exposure in Northeast, mid-Atlantic, upper Midwest; attached blacklegged tick
Tick exposure may be unnoticed; small-mammal reservoirs sustain transmission

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Erythema migrans**: enlarging lesion >5 cm, days after bite; central clearing not required
Early dissemination: multiple lesions, facial palsy, lymphocytic meningitis, fluctuating AV block
Late disease: intermittent large-joint swelling, especially knee; severe pain less prominent than effusion

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Spirochete inoculation → local multiplication, hematogenous spread, inflammatory injury
Persistent antibodies can remain after cure and do not prove viable infection

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical erythema migrans → **clinical diagnosis**, no serology needed
Other compatible disease → two-tier serology: EIA followed by immunoblot or second EIA
Early localized serology may be negative; isolated IgM after >30 days is unreliable
Joint-fluid PCR supports selected arthritis cases; CSF testing for CNS disease; ECG for cardiac symptoms

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Localized skin disease → **doxycycline 10 days**, or amoxicillin/cefuroxime 14 days
Facial palsy/mild neurologic disease may use oral doxycycline; severe CNS disease → IV ceftriaxone
★ Symptomatic carditis, PR ≥300 ms, higher-degree block → **hospitalize, telemetry, IV ceftriaxone**; pacing if needed
Lyme arthritis → 28-day oral course; persistent objective disease requires reassessment, sometimes IV ceftriaxone
Post-treatment nonspecific fatigue → supportive evaluation; no prolonged antibiotics without objective reinfection/failure

rows.label: Complications
items: Complete heart block, meningoencephalitis, recurrent arthritis, postinfectious joint inflammation
Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction shortly after antibiotics; not necessarily drug allergy

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ High-risk Ixodes bite, attachment ≥36 hours, endemic region → **single-dose doxycycline within 72 hours of removal**
Tick checks, permethrin-treated clothing, DEET; remove tick with fine tweezers near skin
No prophylaxis for low-risk bite or routine serologic testing of asymptomatic patients

rows.label: Mimics
items: Immediate bite hypersensitivity: small, itchy, does not progressively enlarge
Septic arthritis: marked pain, toxicity, positive culture; babesiosis: hemolysis and intraerythrocytic parasites

macrocytic-anemia.name: Macrocytic anemia
macrocytic-anemia.scope: Folate deficiency, vitamin B12 deficiency, pernicious anemia, hypersegmented neutrophils, methylmalonic acid and homocysteine
macrocytic-anemia.core: MCV >100 fL prompts separation of megaloblastic DNA-synthesis failure from alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, reticulocytosis, and marrow disorders.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Vegan diet without supplementation, gastric bypass, ileal disease/resection, metformin → B12 depletion
Alcohol misuse, poor intake, pregnancy, methotrexate, trimethoprim → folate depletion
Autoimmune gastritis → pernicious anemia; nitrous oxide functionally inactivates cobalamin

rows.label: Clues
items: Fatigue, pallor, glossitis; ineffective erythropoiesis may raise LDH/indirect bilirubin and lower other cell lines
★ **Paresthesias, gait ataxia, impaired vibration/proprioception** → B12 deficiency, even without anemia
Smooth macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils indicate megaloblastic change

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Defective thymidine synthesis delays nuclear maturation relative to cytoplasm
B12-dependent myelin metabolism explains spinal cord/peripheral nerve injury; folate deficiency lacks this syndrome

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CBC, smear, reticulocytes, B12**; assess folate, liver tests, TSH, exposures
Borderline B12 → methylmalonic acid; renal impairment can elevate it independently
★ Suspected pernicious anemia → **anti-intrinsic-factor antibodies**; highly specific but not fully sensitive
High reticulocytes → bleeding/hemolysis; unexplained cytopenias/dysplasia → bone marrow evaluation for MDS
Coexisting iron deficiency may normalize MCV; neurologic suspicion still requires B12 evaluation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Replace B12 before or with folate**; folate alone can conceal ongoing neurologic injury
Neurologic/severe deficiency or malabsorption → parenteral B12 initially; irreversible cause requires lifelong replacement
Dietary B12 deficiency may respond to high-dose oral replacement; folate deficiency → oral folic acid
Remove causative drug/exposure where possible; monitor reticulocyte response and count recovery

rows.label: Complications
items: Untreated B12 deficiency → irreversible neurologic disability; severe disease → pancytopenia
Pernicious anemia → increased gastric adenocarcinoma and neuroendocrine tumor risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Reliable B12 supplementation for vegans**; lifelong monitoring/replacement after relevant GI surgery
Folic acid before conception and early pregnancy; improve nutrition and reduce harmful alcohol intake

rows.label: Mimics
items: Alcohol-associated macrocytosis: round macrocytes, no required megaloblastic change
Myelodysplasia: persistent multilineage cytopenia, dysplastic marrow
Reticulocytosis: polychromasia after blood loss or hemolysis

macrocytic-anemia.evidence: Not checked online; established hematology and nutritional teaching.

meningitis.name: Meningitis
meningitis.scope: Bacterial meningitis, viral meningitis, fungal/cryptococcal meningitis, CSF interpretation, empiric antimicrobial therapy, chemoprophylaxis
meningitis.core: Fever, headache and meningeal symptoms require prompt CSF evaluation when safe; suspected bacterial meningitis demands antibiotics without imaging-related delay.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Neonates: GBS, E. coli, Listeria; older adults/immunocompromised: additional Listeria risk
Crowding/asplenia → meningococcus; CSF leak → pneumococcus; advanced HIV/transplant → Cryptococcus

rows.label: Clues
items: Neck stiffness, photophobia, vomiting; infants may show poor feeding, irritability or bulging fontanelle
★ Petechiae/purpura with shock → **meningococcemia**; absence of rash does not exclude
Confusion, seizure or focal deficit raises encephalitis, raised-pressure or complicated infection concern

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Organisms reach meninges hematogenously or through contiguous spread/CSF defect; inflammation increases edema and pressure

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Blood cultures → LP** with opening pressure, cell count, glucose, protein, Gram stain/culture and PCR
CT before LP for focal deficit, papilledema, new seizure, marked consciousness impairment or significant immunocompromise
★ If LP delayed: cultures then **immediate antibiotics**; CT cannot rule out every pressure hazard
Cryptococcus: CSF antigen/culture and opening pressure; TB studies for subacute low-glucose lymphocytic profile

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Adult empiric → **vancomycin + ceftriaxone**; add ampicillin if >50 or immunocompromised
Neonate → ampicillin + cefotaxime; avoid ceftriaxone in neonates
Dexamethasone before/with first antibiotic when pneumococcal meningitis suspected; narrow treatment by organism
Cryptococcal meningitis → liposomal amphotericin B + flucytosine, then fluconazole; serial therapeutic LPs for pressure
Uncomplicated viral meningitis → supportive care; suspected HSV encephalitis → IV acyclovir

rows.label: Complications
items: Hearing loss, seizures, hydrocephalus, stroke, cognitive impairment; meningococcus → DIC/adrenal hemorrhage

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Meningococcal close contacts → **rifampin or ceftriaxone** promptly; droplet isolation until 24 hours effective treatment
Hib prophylaxis for qualifying households/childcare; no routine pneumococcal contact antibiotics
Pneumococcal, Hib and meningococcal vaccination; correct recurrent CSF leaks

rows.label: Mimics
items: SAH: thunderclap headache; CT/LP hemorrhagic findings
Encephalitis: parenchymal dysfunction, focal deficits or prominent behavioral change

meningitis.evidence: Contact prophylaxis checked 2026-10-30: [CDC meningococcal guidance](https://www.cdc.gov/surv-manual/php/table-of-contents/chapter-8-meningococcal-disease.html); empiric regimens established teaching.

mitochondrial-disorders.name: Mitochondrial disorders
mitochondrial-disorders.scope: MELAS, MERRF, Kearns-Sayre syndrome, Leber hereditary optic neuropathy, maternal inheritance, heteroplasmy, ragged red fibers
mitochondrial-disorders.core: Multisystem disease involving energy-demanding tissues, with variable severity among maternal relatives, suggests mitochondrial dysfunction.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Mitochondrial DNA variants transmitted maternally; affected fathers do not transmit mtDNA disease
Large mtDNA deletions often sporadic; nuclear mitochondrial disorders may follow Mendelian inheritance

rows.label: Clues
items: Short stature, exercise intolerance, hearing loss, diabetes, cardiomyopathy or ophthalmoplegia in unusual combinations
★ **Stroke-like deficits crossing vascular territories** with seizures/lactic acidosis favor metabolic cerebral dysfunction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Defective oxidative phosphorylation → ATP failure and reliance on anaerobic metabolism
★ **Heteroplasmy**: mixed normal/mutant mtDNA; tissue thresholds explain variable organ involvement and severity

rows.label: Dx
items: Lactate/pyruvate, CK and organ-directed testing; normal lactate does not exclude disease
★ **Molecular testing** of mtDNA/nuclear genes; blood can miss low-level or tissue-specific variants
Muscle biopsy if genetic diagnosis unresolved: ragged red fibers and respiratory-chain abnormalities
Brain MRI for focal symptoms; ECG/echo, hearing, vision and endocrine assessment

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Seizures → **levetiracetam** or other suitable antiseizure drug; avoid valproate, especially POLG-associated disease
Acute stroke-like episode → urgent EEG, seizure treatment, metabolic support; exclude true vascular stroke
MELAS arginine: historical treatment; 2026 consensus finds benefit unproven; specialist-directed use
Kearns-Sayre conduction disease → early cardiology/pacemaker assessment; LHON → specialist consideration of idebenone
Individualized aerobic conditioning, nutrition and organ support; no universal curative regimen

rows.label: Complications
items: Status epilepticus, progressive disability, arrhythmia/sudden death, respiratory failure, permanent visual loss

rows.label: Prevention
items: Genetic counseling including uncertain offspring severity; avoid fasting and severe catabolic stress
Review mitochondrial-toxic drugs; monitor cardiac conduction, glucose, hearing and vision

rows.label: Mimics
items: Embolic stroke: respects arterial territory; vascular source
Myasthenia: fatigable weakness without multisystem metabolic pattern

table.title: Syndromes
rows: Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibers
Onset <20; external ophthalmoplegia, pigmentary retinopathy, block
Young adult; painless subacute central vision loss

mitochondrial-disorders.evidence: MELAS management checked 2026-10-30: [international consensus, 2026](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41999163/); established inheritance/phenotypes.

mononeuropathies.name: Mononeuropathies
mononeuropathies.scope: Ulnar nerve entrapment (cubital tunnel, Guyon canal, claw hand), radial nerve palsy (wrist drop, Saturday night palsy), peroneal/fibular nerve injury (foot drop), electromyography, splinting, surgical decompression
mononeuropathies.core: Weakness and sensory loss following one peripheral nerve suggest focal compression or injury; preserved muscles supplied proximally help localize the lesion.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Compression, fractures, repetitive motion, tight casts, diabetes; intoxicated immobilization → Saturday night radial palsy
Prolonged elbow flexion, cycling/hypothenar pressure, leg crossing, rapid weight loss

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Ulnar: **Froment sign**, advanced fourth/fifth-digit clawing; impaired grip and fine finger tasks
Rapid progression, severe pain, multiple noncontiguous nerves → consider vasculitic mononeuritis multiplex

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Focal compression first causes conduction block/demyelination; severe or sustained pressure causes axonal loss
Axonal regeneration is slow; duration and severity predict recovery

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Map strength, reflexes, and sensation; compare muscles sharing a root but supplied by different nerves
Persistent/uncertain deficit → **EMG/nerve conduction studies**; denervation may take weeks to appear
Trauma → radiographs; suspected mass/structural entrapment → ultrasound or MRI

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Remove compression; activity modification, **splinting**, occupational/physical rehabilitation
Ulnar at elbow → night extension splint; radial palsy → wrist-extension splint
Foot drop → ankle-foot orthosis and gait training; inspect cast/brace pressure points
★ Progressive deficit/refractory entrapment → **surgical decompression**; nerve laceration → urgent repair evaluation

rows.label: Complications
items: Muscle atrophy, fixed contractures, chronic neuropathic pain, falls
Delayed recognition of ongoing compression → irreversible motor deficit

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid prolonged elbow pressure, excessive flexion, leg crossing; pad vulnerable areas during surgery/immobility
Optimize diabetes control; ergonomic adjustment and frequent position changes

rows.label: Mimics
items: L5 radiculopathy: root-pattern pain; weakness also in tibialis posterior and gluteus medius
C8 radiculopathy: additional median-innervated muscle weakness, proximal symptoms
Stroke: sudden deficit with upper motor neuron signs or additional central findings

table.title: Localize common lesions
rows: Palmar ulnar digits; dorsal hand spared
Finger extension; wrist extension partly preserved

mononeuropathies.evidence: Not checked online; established peripheral nerve localization and management.

multiple-sclerosis.name: Multiple sclerosis
multiple-sclerosis.scope: Relapsing-remitting, optic neuritis, transverse myelitis, internuclear ophthalmoplegia (MLF lesion), Uhthoff phenomenon, Lhermitte sign, disease-modifying therapies
multiple-sclerosis.core: Neurologic deficits separated in location and time, often including optic neuritis, suggest inflammatory CNS demyelination.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Young adulthood, female sex, family history; EBV exposure, smoking and low vitamin D association

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Optic neuritis: **pain with eye movement**, monocular visual loss, impaired color vision, afferent pupillary defect
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia: **MLF lesion**, impaired adduction with contralateral abducting nystagmus
Uhthoff: old deficits worsen with heat; Lhermitte: neck flexion triggers electric spinal sensation
Transverse myelitis: weakness, sensory level, urinary dysfunction; acute relapse generally lasts >24 hours

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Immune-mediated oligodendrocyte/myelin injury → CNS plaques, conduction block and eventual axonal loss
Relapsing-remitting: attacks with recovery; progressive forms: accumulating disability between or without attacks

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **MRI brain/cord**: periventricular, cortical/juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal lesions; 2024 criteria add optic nerve
Classic time dissemination: new follow-up lesion or simultaneous enhancing/nonenhancing lesions; exclude better explanation
CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands support diagnosis; revised criteria also accept kappa free-light-chain index
Atypical severe visual loss/long cord lesion → serum AQP4/MOG antibodies; revised criteria permit selected earlier diagnoses
Suspected relapse → exclude fever, UTI and metabolic triggers before escalating immunosuppression

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Disabling relapse → **high-dose methylprednisolone**; severe steroid-refractory attack → plasma exchange
★ Relapsing disease → early disease-modifying drug, e.g., **ocrelizumab**, tailored to activity and pregnancy plans
Lower-activity options include interferon-beta or glatiramer; natalizumab requires JC-virus/PML risk assessment
Baclofen for spasticity; rehabilitation, bladder care and treatment of neuropathic pain
Isolated heat/infection-related worsening → treat trigger; not automatically a new inflammatory attack

rows.label: Complications
items: Gait impairment, falls, neurogenic bladder, depression and cognitive dysfunction
Immunosuppressive treatment → infection; some agents carry PML risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation, exercise, vaccination; review contraception/pregnancy before disease-modifying drugs

rows.label: Mimics
items: B12 deficiency: symmetric posterior-column dysfunction, macrocytosis
NMOSD: AQP4-positive, often severe attacks; some MS drugs worsen disease
Stroke: abrupt maximal deficit, vascular territory

narcolepsy.name: Narcolepsy
narcolepsy.scope: Excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, hypnagogic and hypnopompic hallucinations, sleep paralysis, polysomnography and MSLT, hypocretin (orexin) deficiency, modafinil, sodium oxybate
narcolepsy.core: Irresistible sleep attacks despite sufficient nighttime sleep, with emotion-triggered loss of muscle tone strongly suggesting type 1 narcolepsy.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Usually adolescent/young-adult onset; genetic susceptibility with probable autoimmune hypothalamic neuron loss

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Cataplexy**: seconds to minutes of weakness, preserved consciousness; laughter or surprise trigger
Vivid hallucinations at sleep onset or awakening; transient inability to move at sleep transitions
Short naps refreshing; disrupted nighttime sleep; daytime automatic behaviors

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Type 1: deficient hypothalamic hypocretin/orexin → unstable wakefulness and REM intrusion
Type 2: no cataplexy, no demonstrated orexin deficiency

rows.label: Dx
items: Daily sleepiness ≥3 months; sleep diary/actigraphy first to document sufficient sleep
★ Overnight **polysomnography → next-day MSLT**; exclude untreated OSA and sleep deprivation
Mean sleep latency ≤8 minutes plus ≥2 sleep-onset REM periods; preceding PSG can contribute one
Low CSF hypocretin supports type 1; usually unnecessary with characteristic cataplexy and diagnostic testing
Coordinate stimulant/REM-suppressing drug washout before testing; abrupt withdrawal can confound results

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Daytime sleepiness → **modafinil**; alternatives pitolisant or solriamfetol
★ Prominent cataplexy → **sodium oxybate**; venlafaxine can suppress attacks
Oxybate: avoid alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines because of respiratory/CNS depression
Scheduled naps, regular nighttime sleep, workplace/school accommodations

rows.label: Complications
items: Motor vehicle crashes, impaired school/work performance, depression
Modafinil reduces hormonal contraceptive effectiveness; review pregnancy planning

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid driving or hazardous work until sleepiness controlled; reassess driving safety during follow-up

rows.label: Mimics
items: OSA: snoring, witnessed apneas, abnormal respiratory PSG
Idiopathic hypersomnia: long unrefreshing sleep, fewer sleep-onset REM periods
Syncope/seizure: loss of consciousness or postictal confusion rather than isolated cataplexy

neurocutaneous-disorders.name: Neurocutaneous disorders
neurocutaneous-disorders.scope: Neurofibromatosis type 1, neurofibromatosis type 2, tuberous sclerosis, Sturge-Weber syndrome, von Hippel-Lindau disease, ataxia-telangiectasia
neurocutaneous-disorders.core: Characteristic skin or ocular lesions plus neurologic tumors, seizures, or progressive ataxia suggest an inherited or mosaic multisystem disorder.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: NF1, NF2-related schwannomatosis, TSC, VHL: autosomal dominant; frequent de novo variants
Ataxia-telangiectasia: autosomal recessive; Sturge-Weber: sporadic somatic mosaicism

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Changing painful neurofibroma**, rapid growth, or new weakness → malignant transformation concern
Early focal seizures or developmental regression → evaluate structural cerebral lesions
NF2: hearing loss/tinnitus; NF1: cutaneous neurofibromas and childhood learning difficulties

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Tumor suppressor dysfunction → hamartomas or neoplasms; ATM defect → impaired DNA repair

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical pattern + genetic testing**; targeted MRI for neurologic or tumor symptoms
NF1: ≥2 criteria; ≥6 café-au-lait macules, size >5 mm prepubertal, >15 mm postpubertal
TSC: two major features or one major plus two minor; pathogenic variant also diagnostic

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptomatic tumors → specialist resection; TSC growing lesions → **everolimus** in selected cases
TSC infantile spasms → vigabatrin; other seizures → antiseizure drugs
Sturge-Weber seizures → levetiracetam; refractory focal epilepsy → surgical evaluation
Ataxia-telangiectasia: rehabilitation, infection treatment; minimize ionizing radiation

rows.label: Complications
items: NF1: malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor; VHL: renal carcinoma and pheochromocytoma
TSC: hydrocephalus, renal hemorrhage; ataxia-telangiectasia: lymphoma/leukemia, recurrent sinopulmonary infections

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Genetic counseling**; syndrome-specific eye, hearing, renal, and tumor surveillance
Sturge-Weber: ophthalmology follow-up for glaucoma; NF1: childhood BP and vision monitoring

rows.label: Mimics
items: Isolated café-au-lait macules: no additional diagnostic criteria
Friedreich ataxia: areflexia, cardiomyopathy, no ocular telangiectasias

table.title: Signature findings
rows: Axillary freckling, Lisch nodules, optic glioma
Ash-leaf macules, angiofibromas, cortical tubers, renal angiomyolipomas

neurocutaneous-disorders.evidence: Not checked online; established clinical genetics teaching.

neuromuscular-junction-disorders.name: Neuromuscular junction disorders
neuromuscular-junction-disorders.scope: Myasthenia gravis, Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, botulism, repetitive nerve stimulation, autoantibodies
neuromuscular-junction-disorders.core: Fluctuating or descending weakness with preserved sensation localizes to neuromuscular transmission; reflexes, pupils, and exercise response separate major causes.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: MG: autoimmune disease, thymoma; LEMS: smoking/small-cell lung carcinoma
Botulism: improperly canned foods, injection wounds, infant honey or environmental spores

rows.label: Clues
items: MG: diplopia, ptosis, nasal speech, chewing fatigue; worse late day or repeated activity
LEMS: proximal leg weakness, dry mouth, constipation; transient strength/reflex improvement after exertion
Botulism: cranial palsies → symmetric descending paralysis, autonomic dysfunction; infant constipation and floppy weakness
★ **Bulbar weakness or declining ventilation** → impending respiratory failure even with normal oxygen saturation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: MG: postsynaptic receptor/MuSK autoimmunity; LEMS: presynaptic voltage-gated calcium-channel autoimmunity
Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins → impaired acetylcholine release

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **AChR antibodies**, then MuSK if negative; repetitive nerve stimulation or single-fiber EMG
MG → chest CT for thymoma; bedside ice-pack improvement supports ocular disease
LEMS → P/Q calcium-channel antibodies and chest CT for cancer
★ Suspected crisis → serial **forced vital capacity/negative inspiratory force**; not pulse oximetry alone
Botulism → serum/stool/toxin testing via public health; treatment before confirmation

rows.label: Tx
items: MG → pyridostigmine, steroid-sparing immunosuppression; thymectomy for thymoma or selected generalized AChR-positive disease
★ Myasthenic crisis → **airway support + IVIG or plasma exchange**, treat precipitant
LEMS → amifampridine and treatment of malignancy; immunotherapy for persistent autoimmune disease
★ Botulism → **heptavalent antitoxin**; infants → human botulism immune globulin; ventilatory support
Wound botulism → debridement/antibiotics; avoid aminoglycosides and magnesium with impaired junctional transmission

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration, respiratory arrest; MG immunosuppression → infection; steroids may initially worsen weakness

rows.label: Prevention
items: Review MG-exacerbating drugs; safe food preservation; no honey before age 1 year
LEMS → ongoing cancer surveillance if initial evaluation negative

rows.label: Mimics
items: Guillain-Barré: usually ascending weakness and areflexia, possible sensory symptoms
Brainstem stroke: abrupt focal signs; motor neuron disease: fasciculations/UMN signs

neuromuscular-junction-disorders.evidence: Botulism checked 2026-10-30: [CDC clinical guidelines](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/70/rr/rr7002a1.htm); MG/LEMS: established teaching.

obstructive-sleep-apnea.name: Obstructive Sleep Apnea
obstructive-sleep-apnea.scope: risk factors, clinical features (excessive daytime sleepiness, snoring), polysomnography, CPAP, cardiovascular complications
obstructive-sleep-apnea.core: Recurrent upper-airway obstruction during sleep causes intermittent hypoxemia and arousals, often presenting as loud snoring and excessive daytime sleepiness.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Obesity, large neck circumference, male sex, aging, retrognathia and upper-airway crowding
Alcohol/sedatives worsen collapse; children often have adenotonsillar hypertrophy; risk rises after menopause

rows.label: Clues
items: Witnessed apneas, gasping/choking, unrefreshing sleep, morning headache, nocturia
Resistant hypertension, atrial fibrillation or recurrent drowsy-driving episodes raise suspicion
Children may show hyperactivity, learning problems, enuresis or poor growth rather than sleepiness
Normal awake oxygen saturation does not exclude severe nocturnal disease

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Sleep-related reduction in pharyngeal tone collapses vulnerable airway despite persistent respiratory effort
Intermittent hypoxia and sympathetic surges drive hypertension; fragmentation impairs attention and vigilance

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Polysomnography** confirms; screening tools such as STOP-BANG estimate risk, not diagnosis
Uncomplicated high-risk adults → home sleep apnea test acceptable; negative/inconclusive → in-laboratory study
★ AHI **≥5/hour with symptoms/comorbidity**, or ≥15 regardless of symptoms, establishes adult OSA
AHI 5–14 mild, 15–29 moderate, ≥30 severe; pediatric thresholds differ
Cardiorespiratory disease, suspected hypoventilation, chronic opioids or neuromuscular weakness → laboratory polysomnography

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **CPAP** for symptomatic OSA and most moderate/severe disease; optimize mask fit/adherence
Weight loss, exercise, lateral sleep positioning; avoid bedtime alcohol and sedatives
★ CPAP-intolerant or selected mild/moderate disease → **mandibular advancement device**
Children with adenotonsillar hypertrophy → adenotonsillectomy; selected adults → airway surgery or hypoglossal stimulation
Counsel sleepy patients to avoid driving until controlled; do not rely on stimulants before treating obstruction

rows.label: Complications
items: Systemic hypertension, arrhythmias, stroke risk, pulmonary hypertension in selected patients
Motor vehicle/work accidents, impaired cognition, mood disturbance and perioperative airway risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: Maintain healthy weight, reassess after major weight change; continue PAP around surgery with monitoring

rows.label: Mimics
items: Central apnea: absent respiratory effort during pauses
Narcolepsy: cataplexy and sleep-onset REM features
OHS: persistent daytime hypercapnia

palliative-and-hospice-care.name: Palliative and hospice care
palliative-and-hospice-care.scope: Hospice eligibility, pain control, goals of care, surrogate requests
palliative-and-hospice-care.core: Palliative care relieves suffering at any illness stage; hospice centers care on comfort when prognosis and patient goals support a terminal-care benefit.

rows.label: Principle
items: ★ **Patient goals and informed consent** guide intervention burdens; symptom relief remains an obligation
Proportionate opioids for pain/dyspnea ethically permissible despite foreseeable unintended risks

rows.label: Do
items: ★ Ask understanding/values → discuss prognosis → recommend a goal-concordant plan
Assess capacity; use advance directive, then authorized surrogate: substituted judgment/best interests
★ Titrate **opioids** to symptoms; add stimulant laxative for constipation, reassess sedation/respiration

rows.label: Don't
items: DNR ≠ no antibiotics, fluids, nutrition or other desired treatment
Capable patient’s informed wishes override surrogate requests
No nonbeneficial interventions; explain reasoning, offer alternatives, seek ethics review for conflict

rows.label: Exceptions
items: Refractory terminal suffering → proportional palliative sedation, specialist review and consent
Emergency, unknown preferences → stabilize while clarifying wishes; honor documented refusals

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Hospice: **≤6-month prognosis** if usual course; longer survival permits recertification
Medicare hospice election concerns terminal-illness treatment; unrelated conditions remain treatable
No DNR requirement for hospice; enrollment can be revoked if goals change

palliative-and-hospice-care.evidence: Eligibility checked 2026-10-30: [CMS hospice benefit](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/payment/fee-for-service-providers/hospice); clinical ethics: established teaching.

physician-patient-communication.name: Physician-patient communication
physician-patient-communication.scope: Medical interpreters, limited English proficiency, delivering bad news, empathetic communication, family requests to withhold information
physician-patient-communication.core: Respect autonomy through understandable, honest, empathic dialogue; identify what patients understand and want before sharing decisions or sensitive information.

rows.label: Principle
items: Confidentiality, cultural humility, informed choice; language barriers never imply impaired capacity
Patient preferences determine family involvement and desired level of disclosure

rows.label: Do
items: ★ **Qualified medical interpreter**, free to patient; speak directly to patient in short segments
★ Bad news: privacy → understanding/preferences → warning → plain disclosure → empathy → plan
Validate emotion; open questions, silence, teach-back; explore beliefs before correcting misinformation

rows.label: Don't
items: Avoid jargon, false reassurance, interrupting, arguing, blaming, or premature advice
Avoid routine reliance on children/family for interpreting consent or sensitive discussions
Avoid promising cure or confidentiality beyond legal limits

rows.label: Exceptions
items: ★ **Family requests nondisclosure → ask patient privately**; patient preferences control disclosure
Capable patient may decline details or designate another recipient; document preference
Emergency without interpreter → temporary available help while securing qualified interpretation

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Therapeutic privilege is narrow**; anticipated distress alone never justifies withholding diagnosis
Anger → acknowledge concern, clarify cause, establish boundaries if threatening; no reflex discharge
Requested adult-family interpreter → verify suitability/privacy/voluntariness; offer professional

physician-patient-communication.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [HHS interpreter guidance](https://www.hhs.gov/civil-rights/for-individuals/faqs/may-an-lep-person-use-a-family-member-as-an-interpreter/index.html); established autonomy and bad-news communication principles.

primary-headaches.name: Primary headaches
primary-headaches.scope: Migraine, tension-type, cluster, medication-overuse headache, red flags
primary-headaches.core: Recurrent stereotyped headaches with normal neurologic examination favor a primary syndrome; a new dangerous pattern requires secondary-cause evaluation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Family history, sleep disruption, stress, hormonal fluctuation; alcohol triggers cluster bouts
Frequent rescue analgesic use promotes chronic daily headache

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Thunderclap, fever, papilledema, focal deficit, cancer, pregnancy/postpartum** → evaluate secondary cause
New headache after age 50, positional/Valsalva provocation, progressive change also concerning
Medication overuse: headache ≥15 days/month with sustained frequent acute-drug exposure

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Migraine: trigeminovascular activation/CGRP signaling; aura reflects cortical spreading depolarization
Cluster: hypothalamic/autonomic activation; overuse sustains sensitization and rebound symptoms

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical stable primary pattern + normal exam → **no routine neuroimaging**
Thunderclap → head CT; negative with persistent SAH concern → LP or CTA
MRI for concerning nonemergent progressive patterns; fundoscopy and full neurologic examination
Overuse >3 months: triptans/opioids/combinations ≥10 days/month; acetaminophen/NSAIDs ≥15 days/month

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Severe migraine → **sumatriptan + naproxen**, metoclopramide for nausea; avoid triptans with ischemic vascular disease
Frequent/disabling migraine → propranolol, topiramate, or CGRP-directed prevention; avoid topiramate/valproate in pregnancy
★ Cluster attack → **100% oxygen or subcutaneous sumatriptan**; prevention with verapamil, ECG monitoring
Tension headache → acetaminophen/NSAID; recurrent chronic disease → amitriptyline, behavioral treatment
Medication overuse → withdraw culprit, start prevention; taper opioids/barbiturates rather than abrupt withdrawal

rows.label: Complications
items: Chronic migraine, functional disability, status migrainosus; analgesic toxicity
Estrogen-containing contraception increases stroke concern in migraine with aura

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Regular sleep/meals, exercise, headache diary**, limit rescue-drug days
Avoid opioids for routine primary headache; identify personal rather than universal dietary triggers

rows.label: Mimics
items: GCA: age >50, jaw claudication/visual symptoms
Acute glaucoma: red painful eye, halos, high pressure; sinusitis: purulence and objective sinus findings

primary-headaches.evidence: Not checked online; established headache classification and generalist management.

prion-disease.name: Prion disease
prion-disease.scope: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (sporadic, familial, variant), rapidly progressive dementia, startle myoclonus, ataxia, 14-3-3 protein, RT-QuIC, periodic sharp wave complexes, spongiform encephalopathy
prion-disease.core: Cognitive decline over weeks to months with stimulus-sensitive jerks and cerebellar dysfunction suggests Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Sporadic CJD usually older adults; familial cases involve autosomal dominant PRNP variants
Iatrogenic: contaminated neurosurgical equipment/tissue; variant CJD: bovine spongiform encephalopathy-contaminated beef

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Rapid progression** to akinetic mutism; visual, pyramidal, or extrapyramidal abnormalities
Startle myoclonus often develops after initial behavioral or memory changes
Variant CJD: younger age, early psychiatric symptoms and painful sensory complaints; prolonged course

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Misfolded protein templates conversion of normal prion protein; no nucleic acid
Neuronal loss, gliosis and vacuolation → spongiform encephalopathy without prominent inflammation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Brain **MRI DWI**: cortical ribboning and caudate/putamen diffusion restriction
★ CSF **RT-QuIC** detects abnormal prion seeding; high specificity
CSF 14-3-3 reflects rapid neuronal injury; supportive but nonspecific
EEG: periodic sharp wave complexes; absence does not exclude disease
Exclude treatable mimics: CSF inflammatory/infectious studies, metabolic testing, autoimmune evaluation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Supportive/palliative care**; no established disease-modifying treatment
Clonazepam or levetiracetam for distressing myoclonus; nutrition and caregiver support
Brain biopsy rarely needed; notify infection control before invasive tissue procedures

rows.label: Complications
items: Dysphagia, aspiration, immobility; sporadic CJD usually fatal within one year

rows.label: Prevention
items: Prion-specific instrument decontamination or disposal; routine sterilization insufficient
Familial disease → genetic counseling; casual contact does not transmit CJD

rows.label: Mimics
items: Autoimmune encephalitis: seizures, inflammatory findings; potentially immunotherapy-responsive
Alzheimer disease: progression over years
Wernicke encephalopathy: malnutrition, ophthalmoplegia; treat promptly with IV thiamine

prion-disease.evidence: Diagnosis checked 2026-10-30: [CDC CJD overview](https://www.cdc.gov/creutzfeldt-jakob/hcp/clinical-overview/index.html); established supportive care.

somatic-symptom-disorders.name: Somatic symptom disorders
somatic-symptom-disorders.scope: Somatic symptom disorder, illness anxiety disorder, conversion disorder, factitious disorder, malingering, regular scheduled visits, validating suffering
somatic-symptom-disorders.core: Distressing symptoms or health fears require a positive psychiatric formulation, validation, and proportionate medical evaluation; intent separates factitious behavior from functional symptoms.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Trauma, anxiety/depression, chronic illness, major stress; medical and psychiatric disorders can coexist

rows.label: Clues
items: Persistent reassurance seeking, repeated testing, high health-related distress, impaired function
Assess suicidality, abuse, substance use, and medication-related symptoms; avoid assumptions based on demographics

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Attention, threat appraisal, and learned responses amplify suffering; symptoms do not require conscious production
External reward differs from internal sick-role motivation; neither can be inferred from one inconsistency

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Somatic symptom disorder does not require medically unexplained symptoms**; excessive response is decisive
Illness anxiety requires ≥6 months preoccupation; somatic symptom persistence typically >6 months
★ Functional neurologic disorder: **positive incompatible examination signs**, such as Hoover sign, support diagnosis
New objective abnormalities still warrant targeted medical evaluation; avoid diagnosing solely by exhaustive exclusion

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **One clinician, scheduled visits**, focused examinations; validate suffering without endorsing unproven disease
CBT, functional rehabilitation, treat comorbid anxiety/depression; explain functional neurologic mechanisms nonjudgmentally
★ Avoid repeated low-value procedures; **new red flags → reassess**, regardless of established psychiatric diagnosis
Factitious: coordinated team, factual records, supportive discussion; protect dependents from induced illness

rows.label: Complications
items: Iatrogenic injury, unnecessary surgery, opioid exposure, disability, fragmented care
Factitious disorder imposed on another → serious abuse risk requiring safeguarding action

rows.label: Mimics
items: Occult medical disease: evolving objective findings or coherent physiologic abnormalities
Delusional disorder: fixed somatic belief despite evidence, without flexible doubt

table.title: Distinguishing patterns
rows: Motor/sensory symptoms incompatible with neurologic disease
Intentional deception; no obvious external reward
