spinal-cord-compression.name: Spinal cord compression
spinal-cord-compression.scope: Neoplastic spinal cord compression (epidural metastases, dexamethasone, emergent MRI), spinal epidural abscess (fever, IV drug use, empiric antibiotics), cauda equina syndrome, surgical decompression
spinal-cord-compression.core: Back pain with new weakness, sensory changes or sphincter dysfunction requires urgent MRI to identify reversible neural compression.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Known breast, prostate, lung, renal cancer or myeloma → epidural metastases
IV drug use, bacteremia, diabetes, spinal procedure or immunosuppression → epidural abscess
Large lumbar disc herniation, trauma or spinal stenosis → cauda equina compression

rows.label: Clues
items: Progressive nocturnal pain, pain with cough/strain, radicular symptoms; deficits may be initially subtle
Cord lesion: sensory level, spastic weakness, hyperreflexia below lesion after acute phase
★ Cauda equina: **saddle anesthesia, urinary retention**, reduced anal tone, asymmetric flaccid leg weakness
Epidural abscess: fever/back pain ± deficit; classic triad often incomplete

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Epidural tumor, infection or disc material compresses neural tissue and impairs blood supply
Longstanding compression produces irreversible ischemic injury; bladder dysfunction signals advanced disease

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Urgent contrast MRI** of suspected region; whole spine for suspected metastatic compression
Postvoid residual supports retention assessment but normal result does not exclude early cauda equina syndrome
Suspected abscess → blood cultures, CBC, ESR/CRP; image before LP
MRI unavailable/contraindicated → CT myelography; ordinary radiographs cannot exclude epidural pathology

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Malignant compression with deficit → **dexamethasone immediately**, urgent neurosurgery/radiation consultation
Tumor → decompression/stabilization ± radiotherapy; choice depends on stability, neurologic function and prognosis
★ Epidural abscess → **vancomycin + cefepime**, cultures; urgent decompression for deficits or instability
Cauda equina syndrome → emergency spinal surgical assessment and **decompression**
Immobilize if instability suspected; bladder drainage and analgesia during definitive treatment

rows.label: Complications
items: Permanent paralysis, bowel/bladder dysfunction, sexual dysfunction, pressure injuries and VTE
Abscess → sepsis; steroids can worsen uncontrolled infection

rows.label: Prevention
items: Rapid assessment of cancer-associated new back pain; sterile procedures and prompt bacteremia treatment

rows.label: Mimics
items: Mechanical strain: normal neurologic exam, no sphincter symptoms
Transverse myelitis: intrinsic cord lesion without external compression
Peripheral neuropathy: distal symmetric findings without sensory level

spinal-cord-compression.evidence: Not checked online; established neurologic and oncologic emergency principles.

substance-use-disorders.name: Substance use disorders
substance-use-disorders.scope: Diagnostic criteria (mild, moderate, severe), cocaine use disorder, amphetamine use disorder, cannabis use disorder, motivational interviewing, cognitive behavioral therapy, 12-step programs
substance-use-disorders.core: A problematic pattern causing impaired control, risky use, social impairment or physiologic adaptation defines substance use disorder; severity follows criterion count.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Family history, trauma, psychiatric comorbidity, early exposure, unstable housing and peer availability
Persistent psychosocial stress and limited treatment access worsen trajectory

rows.label: Clues
items: Tolerance/withdrawal not required; physiologic adaptation during prescribed use alone does not establish disorder
Stimulant withdrawal: fatigue, hypersomnia, depression and craving; assess suicide risk
Cannabis withdrawal: irritability, anxiety, insomnia and reduced appetite after sustained use

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Reward learning and neuroadaptation strengthen cue-driven behavior while impairing control
Cocaine blocks monoamine reuptake; amphetamines increase release; cannabinoids act mainly at CB1 receptors

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **≥2 of 11 DSM-5 criteria in 12 months**; assess functional consequences nonjudgmentally
★ Severity: **mild 2–3, moderate 4–5, severe ≥6**
Clinical interview establishes disorder; urine drug testing documents exposure, not severity or current impairment
Screen co-occurring depression, psychosis, HIV/hepatitis risk and polysubstance use; confirm unexpected immunoassay positives

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Motivational interviewing**: explore ambivalence, elicit personal goals, support autonomy; avoid confrontation
★ Stimulant disorder → **contingency management**, CBT/community reinforcement; no FDA-approved maintenance drug
Cannabis disorder → motivational enhancement, CBT and contingency management; no established approved medication
Peer/12-step programs as adjuncts; tailor outpatient versus residential intensity to safety/support and impairment
Acute stimulant agitation → benzodiazepines/cooling; cannabis hyperemesis → cessation, fluids, selected capsaicin/haloperidol

rows.label: Complications
items: Cocaine/amphetamine → MI, stroke, arrhythmia, psychosis; chronic methamphetamine → cardiomyopathy and dental injury
Cannabis → impaired driving, hyperemesis, anxiety or psychosis in susceptible individuals
Stimulant crash can precipitate severe depression/suicidality; withdrawal usually lacks alcohol-like autonomic danger

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Harm reduction: **naloxone** for possible opioid contamination, avoid using alone, offer fentanyl testing access
Treat comorbid illness, relapse planning, overdose education and regular follow-up; recurrence prompts reassessment

rows.label: Mimics
items: Bipolar mania: episodes persist independently of intoxication
Primary psychosis: symptoms outside substance exposure periods
ADHD: longstanding childhood-onset pattern, not episodic intoxication

substance-use-disorders.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ASAM/AAAP stimulant guideline 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11105801/); DSM-5 criteria established definitions.

syphilis.name: Syphilis
syphilis.scope: Primary syphilis, secondary syphilis, latent syphilis, tertiary syphilis, neurosyphilis, serologic testing, Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction, penicillin therapy
syphilis.core: Treponema pallidum infection progresses through mucocutaneous, asymptomatic, and destructive stages; neurologic, ocular, or auditory disease can occur anytime.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Unprotected sex, multiple partners, HIV; transplacental transmission during pregnancy

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Primary: **painless chancre** with regional lymphadenopathy
Secondary: palms/soles rash, condylomata lata, generalized nodes, patchy alopecia
Tertiary: gummas, ascending aortic aneurysm; tabes dorsalis or dementia
Latent: reactive serology without symptoms; early = acquired within 1 year

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Spirochete dissemination → endarteritis; posterior column injury → sensory ataxia

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **RPR/VDRL + treponemal assay**; discordant reverse screen → second treponemal assay
Early chancre with negative serology → lesion testing or repeat serology
★ Neurologic deficits → **LP**; CSF-VDRL specific, negative result does not exclude
Quantitative RPR: early disease follow-up at 6/12 months; latent at 6/12/24 months
Tertiary disease → CSF assessment before treatment; isolated ocular/otic disease may not require LP

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Pregnancy with penicillin allergy → **desensitization**, then stage-specific penicillin
Nonpregnant penicillin allergy, uncomplicated early infection → doxycycline for 14 days

rows.label: Complications
items: Jarisch-Herxheimer: fever/myalgias within 24 hours after treatment; supportive care, not allergy
Congenital infection → stillbirth, hearing loss, dental/bone abnormalities

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Partners exposed within **90 days** → presumptive early-syphilis treatment despite negative tests
HIV testing; prenatal screening; serial RPR after treatment, fourfold rise suggests reinfection/failure

rows.label: Mimics
items: Chancroid: painful ulcer, tender suppurative nodes
HSV: painful grouped vesicles; pityriasis rosea: herald patch, usually spares palms
Autoimmune false-positive RPR: negative confirmatory treponemal assay

syphilis.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [CDC STI guidance](https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/syphilis.htm), including linked stage-specific guidance.

transient-global-amnesia.name: Transient global amnesia
transient-global-amnesia.scope: Anterograde amnesia, repetitive questioning, preserved personal identity, triggers (emotional stress, Valsalva, cold water immersion), clinical diagnosis, self-limited course, benign prognosis
transient-global-amnesia.core: An awake middle-aged or older adult repeatedly asks the same questions because new memories cannot be retained, then recovers within hours.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age usually 50–70; migraine history; emotional stress, exertion, Valsalva, sexual activity or cold-water immersion
Often a witnessed isolated event; no required vascular risk factor pattern

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Personal identity and alertness preserved**; fluent speech, intact familiar skills
Anterograde memory severely impaired; variable recent retrograde loss, immediate span generally preserved
No focal neurologic deficit, seizure activity, head injury or clouding of consciousness
Symptoms usually several hours; complete resolution by **24 hours** except a gap for the episode

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Transient hippocampal dysfunction; proposed mechanisms include venous congestion and migraine-related processes

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis with witness history**, complete neurologic examination and bedside glucose
MRI DWI if atypical features, persistent symptoms or uncertain stroke exclusion
Punctate hippocampal diffusion lesions may appear after 24–72 hours; early normal MRI does not exclude TGA
Focal deficits or continuing amnesia beyond a day → urgent alternative-diagnosis evaluation
Brief recurrent episodes, especially on awakening → consider EEG for transient epileptic amnesia

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Reassurance and observation** until recovery; ensure safe supervision during episode
No established drug treatment; antiplatelets or antiseizure drugs not required for typical isolated TGA
Explain temporary inability to retain information to relatives; repeat explanations calmly

rows.label: Complications
items: ★ **Benign prognosis**: no established increased stroke risk from typical TGA itself
Recurrence possible; permanent major cognitive impairment unusual; distress and residual episode memory gap

rows.label: Mimics
items: TIA/stroke: focal deficits or vascular-territory injury; hippocampal stroke can mimic
Transient epileptic amnesia: shorter, recurrent, often on awakening; automatisms or seizure evidence
Dissociative amnesia: autobiographical/identity loss rather than isolated new-learning failure

transient-global-amnesia.evidence: Not checked online; established clinical diagnostic criteria and prognosis.

traumatic-brain-injury.name: Traumatic brain injury
traumatic-brain-injury.scope: Epidural hematoma, subdural hematoma, cerebral contusion, diffuse axonal injury, concussion, elevated ICP
traumatic-brain-injury.core: Head trauma ranges from transient functional disturbance to expanding hemorrhage; serial neurologic deterioration requires urgent imaging and neurosurgical assessment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Falls, crashes, assault, sports; anticoagulation increases bleeding
Older age, alcohol use and cerebral atrophy predispose to bridging-vein injury

rows.label: Clues
items: Headache, vomiting, amnesia; focal deficit or progressive somnolence suggests structural injury
★ **Unilateral fixed dilated pupil + declining consciousness** → uncal herniation
Cushing response: hypertension, bradycardia, irregular breathing; late sign of critically elevated ICP

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Impact/shear → secondary edema, ischemia, excitotoxicity
Rising intracranial volume → reduced cerebral perfusion; hypotension/hypoxia sharply worsen secondary injury

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ ABCs/cervical protection → **GCS, pupils, focal examination**, repeated serially
**Noncontrast head CT** for moderate/severe injury or mild injury with high-risk features
High-risk features: anticoagulation, skull-fracture signs, focal deficit, repeated vomiting, worsening symptoms
GCS 13–15 mild, 9–12 moderate, ≤8 severe; diffuse axonal injury may require MRI

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **GCS ≤8 → intubate** with spinal protection; prevent hypoxemia/hypotension; reverse anticoagulants promptly
Expanding hematoma, mass effect or deterioration → urgent neurosurgical evacuation; observation only with close monitoring
★ Elevated ICP → head elevation, analgesia/sedation, **hypertonic saline or mannitol**; treat sustained ICP >22 mm Hg
Herniation → brief hyperventilation as bridge; avoid routine prophylactic hyperventilation and corticosteroids
Severe/high-risk TBI → levetiracetam for 7 days; refractory ICP → neurosurgical decompression

rows.label: Complications
items: Posttraumatic seizures, chronic cognitive/behavioral impairment, postconcussion syndrome, hydrocephalus
Skull-base fracture → CSF leak/meningitis; avoid nasal instrumentation with suspected basilar fracture

rows.label: Prevention
items: Seatbelts, helmets, fall prevention; avoid alcohol-related injury
Concussion: no same-day sports; relative rest 24–48 hours → graded recovery/clearance

rows.label: Mimics
items: Intoxication: may coexist; exclude intracranial injury before attributing depressed consciousness to substances
Hypoglycemia: immediate glucose testing identifies reversible altered mental status

rows: Temporal impact; middle meningeal artery; lucid interval
Bridging-vein rupture; gradual or acute decline
Crescent; crosses sutures, limited by dural reflections

tuberculosis.name: Tuberculosis
tuberculosis.scope: Latent TB infection screening (PPD, IGRA), treatment regimens, active pulmonary TB, acid-fast bacilli smear and culture, RIPE therapy, extrapulmonary TB (Pott disease)
tuberculosis.core: Chronic cough, weight loss, night sweats, and upper-lobe cavitation suggest contagious pulmonary tuberculosis; latent infection has no active disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Close contact, endemic-area residence, incarceration, homelessness, crowded housing
HIV, TNF inhibitors, transplant, silicosis, diabetes → progression/reactivation risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Hemoptysis, prolonged fever; primary disease may cause hilar adenopathy or pleural effusion
★ **Back pain with vertebral destruction** → Pott disease; miliary spread causes diffuse micronodules

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Airborne bacilli survive in macrophages; cell-mediated granulomas contain infection until immune failure

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Screening: **IGRA** preferred after BCG; TST read induration at 48–72 hours
Positive screening → symptoms + chest radiograph; neither test distinguishes latent from active infection
★ Active suspicion → **sputum NAAT, AFB smear, culture and susceptibility**; collect serial specimens
Negative smear or IGRA does not exclude active TB, especially with immunosuppression
Pott suspicion → spinal MRI, biopsy/culture; assess cord compression

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected contagious disease → **airborne isolation** and public-health notification
Drug-susceptible active TB: 2 months isoniazid/rifampin/pyrazinamide/ethambutol → 4 months isoniazid/rifampin
Eligible pulmonary cases ≥12 years: 4-month isoniazid/rifapentine/moxifloxacin/pyrazinamide-based regimen alternative
Latent: prefer 3-month weekly isoniazid/rifapentine or 4-month rifampin; exclude active disease first
Isoniazid → pyridoxine for neuropathy risk; Pott with neurologic deficit/instability → urgent spinal surgical evaluation

rows.label: Complications
items: Meningitis, adrenal destruction, spinal cord compression, bronchiectasis
INH/rifampin/pyrazinamide: hepatotoxicity; ethambutol: optic neuropathy; rifampin: enzyme induction, orange secretions

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Contact investigation**, latent-treatment completion; directly observed active treatment improves adherence
Review drug interactions and baseline liver risk; monitor visual acuity/color vision with ethambutol

rows.label: Mimics
items: Lung cancer: focal malignant biopsy
Fungal infection: geographic exposure; nontuberculous mycobacteria: species identification distinguishes

rows: HIV, close contacts, transplant, substantial immunosuppression
Exposure-risk groups, comorbidity risks, young children

vertigo.name: Vertigo
vertigo.scope: Peripheral vs central vertigo, benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (Dix-Hallpike, Epley maneuver), vestibular neuritis and labyrinthitis, Meniere disease, vestibular migraine
vertigo.core: Illusion of movement: timing, triggers, hearing findings and neurologic examination distinguish benign vestibular disease from posterior-circulation ischemia.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older age, vascular risk factors → central ischemia; recent viral illness, head injury or migraine history
Ototoxic drugs and ear disease can cause peripheral vestibular injury

rows.label: Clues
items: Peripheral: horizontal-torsional unidirectional nystagmus, reduced with fixation; no focal neurologic deficit
★ **Vertical/direction-changing nystagmus, skew deviation, severe truncal ataxia or focal deficits** → central concern
New unilateral hearing loss with continuous acute vertigo can represent AICA stroke, not simply labyrinthitis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Asymmetric vestibular input → movement illusion and nystagmus; central lesions involve brainstem/cerebellum

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Dix-Hallpike** for triggered episodic symptoms; typical upbeat torsional nystagmus has latency and fatigues
Continuous acute syndrome with spontaneous nystagmus → **HINTS by trained clinician**; not for brief positional episodes
★ Normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus or skew → **stroke evaluation/MRI ± CTA/MRA**
Untrained examiner or concerning findings → MRI; early diffusion imaging may miss posterior stroke
Typical BPPV → no routine imaging; suspected Meniere → audiometry; horizontal positional nystagmus → supine-roll test

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Central concern → urgent **stroke pathway**; negative head CT cannot exclude posterior infarction
Severe acute nausea → brief meclizine/ondansetron; prolonged vestibular suppressants impair compensation

rows.label: Complications
items: Falls, dehydration, impaired driving; missed stroke → disability/death; recurrent inner-ear disease → hearing loss

rows.label: Prevention
items: Fall precautions, avoid driving during attacks; reduce individual migraine triggers and address vascular risk

rows.label: Mimics
items: Orthostatic hypotension: standing-triggered presyncope with BP drop, rather than head-position-triggered nystagmus
Arrhythmia: episodic faintness/palpitations; ECG or monitoring establishes cardiac cause
